name: Mandala
basis: rings of motifs with rotational symmetry (how)
note: Sand mandalas are physical, but no sand or paint is modelled.

lumenary.blurb: A sacred circle in the Buddhist and Hindu tradition: rings built outward from a centre, each with its own repeating shape, picked out in gold line. The colours of every petal come from your picture.

facts.era: Ancient, with sacred forms still made today

why: In the Buddhist and Hindu traditions a mandala is a plan of a sacred world, built from the centre outward in rings. The program has no meaning of its own to give, but it builds the geometry faithfully: a centre, rings that grow outward, and a symmetry that repeats every motif a whole number of times, with the colours of every petal drawn from your picture.
how: Place the centre in the middle of the canvas, and make K rings, each of thickness Δ = R_max/(K + 0.7), reaching the corners.
Give the pattern n₀-fold rotational symmetry, so every ring repeats its motif a whole multiple of n₀ times.
Choose each ring’s count so its motifs are about as wide as the ring is thick, and turn every second ring by half a step so petals sit in the gaps of the ring before it.
Use six motifs in turn: lotus petals, beads, triangles, scallops, diamonds and more.
Colour each motif from the picture, and pick out the lines in gold with a soft glow.
history: The Sanskrit word means circle. Tibetan sand mandalas are made grain by grain over days and then swept away, a teaching about impermanence. Carl Jung, in the early twentieth century, drew mandalas himself and saw them as symbols of wholeness. Similar radial designs are found in many places, from Gothic rose windows to Islamic geometric patterns.
terms: A circular diagram used in Buddhist and Hindu practice.
A shape that looks the same after turning by a certain angle.
The idea that all things change and pass.
paragraphs: The Sanskrit word means “circle”. In the Buddhist and Hindu traditions a mandala is a plan of a sacred world, built from the centre outward in rings, and the sand mandalas of Tibet are made grain by grain and then swept away. The program has no meaning of its own to give them, but it builds the geometry faithfully. The centre is the middle of the canvas, the rings reach to the corners, and there are K of them, each of thickness Δ = R_max/(K + 0.7). The symmetry is n₀-fold rotational: every ring repeats its motif a whole multiple of n₀ times.

A ring’s count is chosen so its motifs are about as wide as the ring is thick, and every second ring is turned by half a step so petals sit in the gaps of the ring before it. Six motifs take turns: lotus petals, beads, triangles, scallops, diamonds and leaf pairs. Each is drawn in the colour of your picture at its own place (or, if you choose to mirror the colours, at the matching place in a single wedge so that the colour pattern is symmetrical too), outlined in gold, with a lighter inner shape. At the heart is a star of n₀ points.

equations.note: The outer radius of ring k.
The number of motifs in a ring of mid radius ρ_m: a multiple of n₀, so each ring is as symmetric as the whole.
Mirrored colours: an angle is folded into a single wedge, where the picture is read, so the colours repeat as the shapes do.

presets.text: Twenty-four-fold symmetry makes a delicate rosette.
Mirror the colours for a calmer, balanced result.
Strong gold lines on maroon give a temple banner look.
